items.prose: Six shares have signal ranks 1 to 6 on a rebalance date. The book uses rank weights: longs sum to +0.5, shorts to −0.5.
items.question: What weight does the top-ranked share get? Give 4 decimal places.

widget.label: Weight
widget.accept: 0.2778: (6 − 3.5)/9, since the sizes of rank − 3.5 add to 9.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the mean rank, 3.5, and divide by the sum of absolute values.

byKey.share: You used rank over the sum of ranks, 6/21. Rank weights subtract the mean rank first.
byKey.equal: You split the long side equally over three shares. Rank weights tilt towards the top.

explain.text: Rank − 3.5 runs −2.5 to 2.5, with sizes adding to 9. The top weight is 2.5/9 = 0.2778, and the three longs sum to 4.5/9 = 0.5.

items.prose: In lesson 13, same-day returns turned daily reversal's Sharpe of 3.42 into −76. The same bug on monthly 12−1 momentum moves its gross Sharpe only from 1.82 to 1.81.
items.question: Why does the bug barely move momentum?

options.text: 12−1 momentum skips the last 21 days, so the one leaked day a month tells it almost nothing
Momentum is immune to look-ahead, because it changes slowly from day to day
options.why: No signal is immune. Here the leaked day carries almost no information about the signal, so the damage is small.

options.text: Monthly rebalancing fixes the bug, because weights are set only 12 times a year
options.why: The bug is still there, on every rebalance day. Small damage is not no damage.

options.text: Momentum's costs hide the change, because they are far larger than one day's return
options.why: Both numbers are gross; there are no costs in either.

feedback.correct: Correct. A small effect is still a bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which day's return leaks, and what the signal knows about it.

explain.text: With monthly weights the bug pays only each rebalance day's return to the new weights, and 12−1 momentum does not contain that day. The alignment test in lesson 13 catches it anyway, which is why tests beat eyeballing Sharpes.

items.prose: A four-share book moves from (0.20, 0.30, −0.30, −0.20) to (0.35, 0.15, −0.10, −0.40) at a rebalance.
items.question: What is the turnover of the rebalance?

widget.label: Turnover
widget.accept: 0.35: the changes 0.15, 0.15, 0.20, 0.20 add to 0.70; half of that.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the absolute changes and halve.

byKey.both: You counted both sides. Turnover is one side.

explain.text: The absolute changes add to 0.70 of the book: 0.35 bought and 0.35 sold. Turnover is 0.35.

items.prose: You must buy £2m of a share that trades £50m a day, with daily volatility 1.5% and a half spread of 3 bp. Use the square-root impact model with $c = 1$.
items.question: What does the trade cost in all, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Impact is $\sigma\sqrt{Q/V}$; add the half spread; apply to £2m.

byKey.spread: You charged only the half spread. A trade of 4% of the day's volume moves the price.
byKey.noroot: You used $\sigma Q/V$. Impact grows with the square root of the share of volume.

explain.text: $Q/V = 0.04$, $\sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$, so impact is 0.015 × 0.2 = 30 bp. With the 3 bp half spread the trade pays 33 bp of £2m, £6,600.

items.prose: Weekly reversal earns 6.37% a year gross and turns over 34.3 times a year.
items.question: What is its break-even cost, in bp per £ traded? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the £ traded on both sides.

byKey.onesided: You divided by the one-sided turnover. Both the buys and the sells pay.

explain.text: £ traded a year is 2 × 34.3 = 68.6 per £ of book, so break-even is 9.3 bp. The median half spread is 7.3 bp, so impact leaves almost nothing.

items.prose: A strategy has a net Sharpe of 1.0 over two years of daily returns, 504 days.
items.question: What is the lower end of its 95% interval by Lo's formula? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Correct. Two years cannot rule out zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compute the SE per day, then annualise it with √252.

byKey.years: You left the SE per day. Annualise it to match the annual Sharpe.
byKey.sign: 1.0 − 1.96 × 0.71 is below zero, because the margin of 1.39 is bigger than the Sharpe of 1. A positive 0.39 takes 1.39 − 1, the wrong way round.

explain.text: The SE is about $1/\sqrt{2} = 0.71$ a year, so the interval is −0.39 to 2.39. A Sharpe of 1 needs about four years before its interval clears zero.

items.prose: A researcher tries 4 lookbacks for a signal, each at 3 rebalance frequencies, all on the same data. Earlier she ran 2 versions with a filter she later dropped.
items.question: How many variants, $N$, go in the note?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the grid, then add every dropped run.

byKey.grid: You left out the dropped versions. They were tried on the same data, so they count.
byKey.sum: You added the settings. Each lookback ran at each frequency: multiply.

explain.text: The grid is 4 × 3 = 12 runs, and the two dropped versions make 14. Runs that were abandoned count as much as the ones kept.

items.prose: Three drafts of one line in a research note's What failed section.
items.question: Which meets the rubric: specific, quantified, no excuses?

options.text: Weekly reversal: gross Sharpe 2.35, net −5.65 at £100m; break-even 9.3 bp per £ traded, close to the median half spread of 7.3 bp.
Weekly reversal did not work out after costs.
options.why: It names the failure but gives no number a reader can check.

options.text: Weekly reversal would have worked with a cheaper broker.
options.why: That is an excuse, and an untested one.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the line a reader could check.

explain.text: The good line says what was tried, what it earned before and after costs, and why in numbers. Another researcher can rerun it.
